description_full: Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp., a shipping company, engages in the seaborne transportation of dry bulk commodities worldwide. It operates 18 Capesize and two Newcastlemax dry bulk vessels with a cargo-carrying capacity of approximately 3,633,861 deadweight tons. The company was formerly known as Seanergy Merger Corp. and changed its name to Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. in July 2008. Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. was incorporated in 2008 and is based in Glyfada, Greece.
ceo_bio: Mr. Stamatios  Tsantanis | Chairman & CEO | Age 53
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 96 people. Revenue per employee of $1.6M ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 17%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $177K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $42K per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp is a small-cap industrials business with a $345M market cap on $158M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +30% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are contracting by -4.5pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 96% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $17M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 26% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 27% operating margin runs 19pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.46x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 101% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 47% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.53 vs 5y 0.71), so read it loosely.
About $5.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 95% in the 2020 crash, 62% in the 2022 bear market and 63% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $24.01, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 27%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $15.53 to $36.57 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 5.5 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 5.7 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 44% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $23.25 on average, 46% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.59).
It runs a 96% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.48x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 14pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 2.6% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.6x net debt to EBITDA ($48.2M of cash against $290.2M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.37 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.85 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.1% over 3 years, 20.1% over 5 years and 29.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 143%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (22.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 28, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 25.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 27%.
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (8.8% in dividends).
The share count has grown 25.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 96 employees, each generates about $1.6M of revenue, 4.5x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 17.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $177K of free cash flow per employee.
